::: {#thm-chocolate}
#### Breaking a chocolate bar takes one break fewer than its squares

For every natural number (@def-natural-numbers) $n$,
splitting a bar of chocolate, a row of $n$ squares, into single squares takes exactly $n - 1$ breaks,
however the breaks are made.

:::

::: {.content-hidden when-format="revealjs"}

{{< slidebreak >}}

::: proof

We use strong induction (@def-strong-induction).
Let $P(n)$ be the claim for a bar of $n$ squares,
let $n$ be a natural number, and suppose $P(k)$ holds for every natural number $k < n$.

If $n = 1$, the bar is already a single square, so it takes $0 = n - 1$ breaks.

If $n \ge 2$, the first break splits the bar into two pieces of $a$ and $b$ squares,
with $a + b = n$, $a \ge 1$ and $b \ge 1$, so $a < n$ and $b < n$.
Each later break splits a single piece, so it falls inside one of these two pieces,
and the later breaks are the breaks of the $a$-square piece together with the breaks of the $b$-square piece.
By the strong induction hypothesis,
the piece of $a$ squares takes $a - 1$ breaks and the piece of $b$ squares takes $b - 1$ breaks.
So the whole bar takes

$$
\ba
1 + (a - 1) + (b - 1)
&= a + b - 1
\\&= n - 1
\ea
$$

breaks.

:::

:::
